title: High Throughput Specimen for in-situ Transmission Electron Microscopy
content: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) is a popular and powerful method for in-situ studies relating to growth and processing of a wide range of materials. Such studies commonly require a substrate onto which the material of interest is deposited and that allows stimuli, commonly heating, to be applied while being imaged by the electron beam. This gives the researcher the ability to measure phenomena such as grain growth, thin film dewetting, Oswald ripening, electromigration, oxidation, catalytic processes or electrochemical phenomena with high spatial, chemical and time resolution. The current state of the art is microheaters on silicon nitride membranes provide rapid and precise heating with compatibility with a wide variety of material systems. However, a limitation of in-situ TEM is the rate at which experiments may be conducted, primarily due to sample preparation, preventing the acquisition of truly statistically robust datasets or adequate probing of parameter space.
